## What caused each symptom

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| 263 orders for 250 units | Every change reads a SKU and writes it back with nothing stopping another call in between, so concurrent calls overwrite each other. `reserve`, `commit` and `addStock` running at the same time on one SKU lose each other's `reserved` updates, which frees stock that is actually held. |
| `reserved` went negative | `release` never checked the order's status, so releasing a committed order took its units off `reserved` a second time. `expire()` made this much worse: it released every old order, including committed and already-released ones, and listed them all as released. Two concurrent releases of one order (say `expire` and a customer cancel) also both went through. |
| Retry held units twice | The check for an existing order and the write of the new one aren't atomic. A retry arriving while the first request's write was still slow found no order and held the stock again. |
| Bundle item stayed held | `reserve` held each item as it checked it, so when a later item was short or unknown, the earlier ones were already held. No order record was written, so not even `expire` could free them. |
| `sold` too high | A commit retried while the first was still running counted the units twice. A commit racing `expire` or `release` could count the units as sold while the order ended up `released`. |

## The fix
- **Per-key locks:** each call that changes state locks its order, then the SKUs it touches, and nothing else. Calls that share no SKU and no order never wait for each other. `available` and `snapshot` take no locks.
  - SKUs are locked in sorted order, and no call ever holds a SKU lock while waiting for an order lock, so two calls can't deadlock.
  - The locks belong to the store object, so two service instances sharing a store also stay out of each other's way.
- **`reserve`** checks every item before holding any, and it's idempotent under concurrent retries.
- **`release`** rejects a committed order with `OrderStateError`, as the doc comment already said it should.
- **`expire`** re-reads each order under its lock and only releases orders that are still `reserved` and older than the TTL.
- **No in-place edits:** the service never modifies objects it gets back from the store, so a store that doesn't copy values is also safe.

**Performance:** 1000 concurrent reserves took 16 ms on 1000 distinct SKUs and 76 ms on one hot SKU, which has to queue. That confirms the fix doesn't bring back the INC-5490 service-wide lock.

## Tests
- There is one test per symptom. The retry cases use a store that stalls one write, which is how a timeout actually happens.
- One test checks that calls on other SKUs and orders finish while another call is stuck.
- A randomized test runs 25 seeds, each with 250 mixed calls, including `expire` releasing orders while commits race against it. At the end it checks every counter against the order records.
- The one new test that passes on the old code fires simultaneous retries. On the old code the double hold and a lost update cancel out, so it can't show the bug. I kept it because it would catch a fix that locks SKUs but not orders.

## Limits you should know about
- **One process only:** the locks work within one Node process, and I assumed the 40 workers share one. If they are separate processes on a shared Redis, this won't coordinate them. That would need atomic store operations (Lua scripts, `WATCH`, `SETNX`), and a store limited to `get`/`set`/`keys` doesn't have them.
- **Store failures aren't rolled back:** if the store fails partway through a call, the writes already made stay in place. A `get`/`set`/`keys` store has no transactions.
- **Existing data isn't repaired:** this change doesn't fix the counters already corrupted in the sale (negative `reserved`, inflated `sold`). Someone will need to run a one-off job that rebuilds them from the order records.

I haven't committed anything.
